docs.text: Silverdash360 ¶ Silverdash360 is a dashboard for the Xbox 360: it lists the games and apps on your console, with their box art, and starts them. It also plays your music, videos and pictures, from the console's drives and from media servers on your network, and shares the console's drives over FTP. It's written in C# on the console's own Silverlight platform with Silverlight360 . docs.text: Contributing ¶ Contributions are welcome: fixes, features, documentation, testing on your console, and good bug reports. Pull requests go to GitHub . Ways to help ¶ Report problems and ideas on GitHub Issues : see Problems and ideas . Test on your console , especially with a large collection, USB drives, media servers or themes that others might not have, and say what works and what doesn't. Improve the docs : every page here has an edit link to its file in the docs folder. Fix something or add a feature with a pull request. Before you start ¶ For a small fix, a pull request on its own is fine. For a new feature or a bigger change, open an issue first, or comment on one that's there, so we can agree on how it should work before you spend time on it. Issues labelled good first issue and help wanted are a good place to start. Making a change ¶ Fork the repository and make a branch from master . Set up the build: the Silverlight360 SDK and a runtime you made yourself (see Development and The runtime ). Make the change, in the style of the code around it. Try it on a console that runs homebrew, or in xenia-edge : a Debug build, tools\deploy.py to put it on the console, and the tests in tests (see Debug server and tests ). Update the docs in docs when you change what users see or do. Open a pull request against master . Pull requests ¶ Keep each one to one change, so it's easy to review; a fix and an unrelated feature are two pull requests. Say what it changes and why, which issue it fixes ( Fixes #12 ), and how you tested it: on which console or in xenia, and which test suites passed. Screenshots help for anything on screen: tools\screenshot.py takes them from a running Debug build (see the tests README ). Commit messages say what the change does, in a short first line, such as "Keep a theme pick for each profile". It needs to build with tools\Build.ps1 -Release without new warnings. What can't go in ¶ The runtime and the donor app's files : default.xex , xcoreclr.dll , the framework assemblies and anything else from the Plex app or Microsoft. They aren't Digiex's to hand out, so they never go in the repository or a release on GitHub. Code or files from the Xbox 360 SDK or from other people's projects whose licenses don't allow it. Anything taken from a console's firmware , such as its dashboard's files: Silverdash360 reads them on the console instead. License ¶ Silverdash360 is licensed under the PolyForm Noncommercial License 1.0.0 with an additional condition. By opening a pull request, you agree that your contribution is licensed under the same terms. Questions ¶ Ask on the Silverdash360 thread on Digiex , or in the issue you're working on.

docs.text: Development ¶ Silverdash360 is C# and XAML for the Xbox 360's Silverlight platform, built with the Silverlight360 SDK. Building ¶ You need what Silverlight360 needs (see its getting started guide ), including a runtime profile (see The runtime ). Then: .\tools\Build.ps1 -Debug -Sdk path\to\Silverlight360 Every build is one of two: -Debug starts with the debug server on (see below) and lands in src\Silverdash360\bin\Debug\xbox\ . tools\deploy.py , tools\Run.ps1 and the tests use it. -Release starts with the debug server off, until Settings > Debug server turns it on, and lands in src\Silverdash360\bin\Release\xbox\ . Builds for others are these. tools\Run.ps1 -Release runs it. Both compile Silverdash360.dll to a native image, Silverdash360.ni.dll , with XboxNGen (the SDK's -NGen ; see its native images page), so the dashboard's code runs compiled instead of through the runtime's IL interpreter: on a console its benchmarks run tens to hundreds of times faster. That runs xenia-edge from the silverlight-build branch of jessenic/xenia-edge ( XENIA_EDGE , or beside the repositories) for a minute or so, and can't while another xenia-edge runs. -NoNGen builds without the image, quicker; that package runs interpreted. The image is unsigned, which the consoles Silverdash360 runs on allow. An image is bound to the exact Silverdash360.dll it was made from: one left beside a newer Silverdash360.dll stops the runtime as it starts. A build always has a matching one or none, and tools\deploy.py , tools\Run.ps1 -Install and the in-app update rename or delete an installed image when what they put in has none. Settings lists XboxNGen while the image is loaded, as XboxNGen's license asks. -AppOnly writes Silverdash360's own files alone, without the runtime and without a native image, into bin\<Debug|Release>\app\ . -Sdk can be left out when the SILVERLIGHT360 environment variable points to the SDK, or when it's cloned next to this repository as Silverlight360 . The package runs as the title the SDK's runtime profile came from (Plex by default), so it's started like that app. The debug server listens on port 4601 without a password, which is why Release builds leave it off: turning it on lets anyone on the network control the dashboard. The runtime ¶ Silverdash360 runs on the Silverlight platform the console's own apps shipped with: the runtime ( default.xex , xcoreclr.dll , agcore.dll and the rest) and its framework assemblies. They're Microsoft's and the donor app's, so GitHub releases have only Silverdash360's own files, and users get the runtime with the base package from the Digiex thread (see Installing ). To build Silverdash360, or to make the base package, make the runtime yourself from the Plex app for Xbox 360, version 0.0.0.7, extracted; the Silverlight360 getting started guide says where to get it and how to extract it. In PowerShell in the Silverlight360 folder: .\tools\New-RuntimeProfile.ps1 -DonorApp 'C:\path\to\Plex v0.0.0.7' -Output .\runtime\plex-2015 The runtime is the runtime\plex-2015\package folder it makes, once for every version of Silverdash360. A build puts it and Silverdash360's files together; so does copying a release zip's files over a copy of that folder. The package's default.xex is the platform's, changed to drop the donor app's title, so it starts only on a console that runs homebrew. Releases ¶ .\tools\Release.ps1 -DryRun .\tools\Release.ps1 Release.ps1 makes a Release build of Silverdash360's own files (the ones the SDK's XboxAppOnly lists, taken from a whole Release package), zips them with an INSTALL.txt , and publishes the zip on GitHub Releases with the commits since the last release as its notes. The zip has no default.xex , runtime or framework assemblies: those are Microsoft's and the donor app's, so whoever installs it lays it over the base package or a runtime profile of their own. The zip has the native image of its Silverdash360.dll too, made in that whole package, and NativeImage.txt , the runtime the image was made against: each of the runtime's native images and xcoreclr.dll , with its size. The base package's runtime is that one (Plex's). The in-app update installs the image only when the files in the dashboard's folder match the record; otherwise it leaves the image out and the dashboard runs interpreted. INSTALL.txt says to leave it out by hand over another runtime. -NoNGen releases without it. Every release has a higher version than the last, tagged v<version> . That's Silverdash360Version in Silverdash360.csproj when it's higher than the last release's, so a minor or major version can be set by hand; otherwise the script raises the last release's patch number (or the part -Bump Minor or -Bump Major names). A new version is committed to the project file and that commit pushed, so the release is built and tagged from it; everything before it has to be committed and pushed already. The release's title has the build number settings shows. The script needs the GitHub CLI ( gh ) signed in. -DryRun shows the version, builds the zip and shows the notes, without committing, pushing or publishing. -Highlight 'Huge performance improvements' puts lines at the top of the notes, above the commits; the update screen shows the notes' first lines. .\tools\Release.ps1 -Console makes the base package that the Digiex thread offers, and releases nothing: the whole Release package, runtime included, in a Silverdash360 folder ( src\Silverdash360\bin\Release\console\Silverdash360-<version>-console.zip ) to copy to the console. It has the donor app's and Microsoft's files, so it's posted on Digiex rather than on GitHub. The documentation ¶ This site is the docs folder, built with MkDocs ( mkdocs.yml ). A push to master that changes it publishes it to GitHub Pages ( .github/workflows/docs.yml ). To preview it: pip install mkdocs==1.6.1 python -m mkdocs serve Debug server and tests ¶ While the debug server is on (from the start in a Debug build; in a Release build once Settings > Debug server turns it on), it takes commands on TCP port 4601, one line each, and answers with a line of JSON: what the library holds, the console's functions called directly, memory, the log, what's on screen, button presses, frame rates and benchmarks of the dashboard's own work. Settings shows its address. The setting is kept, so a build deployed over one with it on starts with it on; it has no password, so anyone on the network can control the dashboard while it's on. python tests/run_tests.py 192.168.1.20 python tests/debugclient.py 192.168.1.20 The first runs the API, functional and performance tests against the console and can compare performance with an earlier run; the second is a shell for typing commands. See tests/README.md for the commands, the protocol and adding tests. To put a new build on the console and start it, over the dashboard's own FTP server and the debug server: python tools/deploy.py 192.168.1.20 -- --suite functional It finds where the dashboard runs from (else /Hdd1/Apps/Silverdash360 ), uploads only the files that changed, starts the new build through a staging folder so no running file is overwritten, checks it came up, and runs the tests given after -- . See Deploying a build . Running in xenia-edge ¶ .\tools\Run.ps1 -Steps '16:shot' -Seconds 20 -ContentRoot gives xenia a content folder of its own, so the dashboard can be tried on a known set of packages without touching xenia's (see Testing in xenia ). The dashboard needs the XAM functions below, which xenia-edge doesn't have yet; they're on the pr-dashboard-content branch, to be proposed to xenia-edge. Function What the dashboard uses it for XamContentAggregateCreateEnumerator Every package of every title, as the console's dashboard lists them XamContentGetMetaDataInternal A package header's names, description and art XamContentLaunchImageInternalEx Starting a package xenia's hard drive has only its Content folder, so a build run from bin\Debug\xbox can't save its library, art or logs. To have it save them, install it under the content folder: -Install copies the build to <ContentRoot>\Silverdash360 and runs it from there, where the dashboard finds itself as /Hdd1/Content/Silverdash360 and keeps its data in Data beside it. -Fresh deletes that Data first, as a new install. .\tools\Run.ps1 -ContentRoot $env:TEMP\testcontent -Install -Fresh To sign a profile in at the start, pass --logged_profile_slot_0_xuid=<offline XUID> in -ExtraArgs ; xenia keeps the flags it's given in its config, so clear that line there to start with nobody signed in again. Signing in and out while the dashboard runs is xenia's Profile menu. The dashboard writes what it does to xenia's log as (DbgPrint) [Silverdash] ... . For the FTP server, run with --systemlink_transport=off (for example .\tools\Run.ps1 -ExtraArgs '--systemlink_transport=off' ): otherwise xenia's System Link emulation carries the dashboard's sockets and nothing listens on the PC. xenia moves port 21 to 10021, and the hard drive has only its Content folder there. How it works ¶ Everything is C#. The console's own functions are called with DllImport by ordinal, with structures passed as pinned big-endian buffers. src/Silverdash360/ Native/ DllImports into xam.xex and xboxkrnl.exe, and NativeBuffer for structures Model/ ContentItem (one package), ContentMetadata (its header), TitleEntry, Gamer, ... Core/ Logging, background work, UiIdle (work that waits for the user), a JSON reader Services/ Library, LibraryCache, ProfileService, ImageService, ThemeService, UpdateService, ... Files/ XboxFileSystem: the drives as one tree of paths Ftp/ FtpServer, FtpSession and NativeSocket Media/ MediaService, the drive, DLNA and downloaded video sources, the local media server, an HTTP client Controls/ TileGrid (the virtualized grid), tile templates, OnScreenKeyboard, Theme Modules/ The hub's sections and the registry they're listed in Pages/ Hub, title details, search, storage, media, the player, pictures, files, themes, updates Debugging/ The debug server and its commands, on by default in Debug builds tests/ The tests that run over the debug server, and a client for it The library is read the way the console's dashboard reads it: Content : XamContentAggregateCreateEnumerator over every title, for common content and for the signed-in profile, returning 0x200-byte XCONTENT_DATA_INTERNAL records: of every type on a first start or a full refresh, otherwise of the types that start games and apps (see below). Metadata : XamContentGetMetaDataInternal per package, for names, description, publisher, version, size and thumbnails. Profile : XamUserGetSigninInfo , XamUserReadProfileSettings for the gamer card, XamUserCreateTitlesPlayedEnumerator and XamUserCreateAchievementEnumerator , and XamReadTile for game tiles and gamer pictures. Launching : XamContentLaunchImageInternalEx with the package's record, after checking it isn't partly downloaded or damaged. An executable from an Apps or Games folder starts with XamLoaderLaunchTitleEx and flags 0, with its folder as the D: drive. FTP : the console's Winsock ( NetDll_socket , bind , listen , accept , ...) on threads of its own, and the kernel's file calls on the drives' device paths. LibraryCache keeps the records and the header metadata in the Data folder of the folder the dashboard is installed in: the console's packages and the Apps and Games executables, the same whoever is signed in, in library.bin , and each profile's own packages (its saves and themes) in Profiles\<offline XUID>.bin . A package is the profile's when the profile's enumeration found it, whatever its record's XUID says. On a start the saved library is shown first, the console's packages with the signed-in profile's. Then only the types that start games and apps, with disc installs and themes, are listed again: on a console each type listed costs about 3 s however few packages it has, plus about 16 ms a package, and those are a few hundred of thousands. Add-ons, saves, avatar items, videos and the rest stay as saved; a title's page lists that title's packages again (an add-on holding an app, as Air Band is, keeps what was found in it), and Refresh library in settings lists everything. Only packages the files don't know have their headers read. With nobody signed in, only the console's are shown. A profile signing in or out from the Guide changes only the profile's part: the new profile's file and enumeration are read, the titles it and the old profile touch are built again (or copied, when only their played stats and saves change), and the console's packages stay as they are. A sign-in during a refresh pauses the refresh until the profile is shown. The debug server's library.profile times that step by step and checks it against a whole build. Reading the library, the art and the Marketplace pause while the user moves ( UiIdle ), and a save is written to a new file before the old one is replaced, so starting a game part way through doesn't lose it. Themes : the theme in use is kept per profile in Data\CurrentTheme\<offline XUID> : its wallpapers and the colours worked out from the first, with theme.txt naming the theme ( package:<title>/<file> or builtin:<n> ). A start reads only the profile's theme choice; when it names the kept theme, the wallpapers and colours come from there, without mounting the package or sampling a wallpaper again. Theme files don't change, so the name is all that's compared. The built-in themes' list is read from the DashPack ( \Device\Harddisk0\SystemExtPartition\Content\0000000000000000\FFFE07DF\00008000\FFFE07DF00000006 on a console) only when the theme picker wants it. A picture theme made in the Xbox Dashboard keeps its wallpaper as raw pixels rather than a JPEG: RGB , the width and height as big-endian words, then red, green and blue bytes a row at a time; WallpaperImage turns those into a WriteableBitmap 's pixels in the background. The theme picked is each profile's too, and nobody signed in's, in Data\ThemeChoice\<offline XUID or Nobody>.txt ; one with no pick follows the Xbox Dashboard's theme, which for nobody signed in is Silverdash's own look. Themes from the editor are kept per profile in Data\CustomTheme and, saved for everyone, in Data\SavedThemes . Media : the platform's player plays only from a URI, so the dashboard serves a file on a drive to it over HTTP on the console itself (port 4602, with a key made up at each start in every URL). A media server's files go through the same server, as the player won't play from another machine. Media servers are found with an SSDP search and browsed through their ContentDirectory; tests/dlna_server.py is a small one for trying it. Updates : the latest release comes from GitHub's API over HTTPS through the platform's HttpWebRequest ( github.com itself doesn't answer the console; api.github.com and its file storage do). The zip is checked against the release's size and SHA-256, its files written next to the dashboard's as .new , each running file renamed to .old (the system allows that for a file in use) and the new one put in its place; a failure puts the old ones back. A release's native image goes in only over the runtime its NativeImage.txt records; without it, the update renames an installed Silverdash360.ni.dll to .old as well, and the dashboard runs interpreted. The dashboard starts again, and the next start deletes the .old files. Debug builds don't look by themselves; the debug server's update.check , update.verify and update.install test it. Extending it ¶ A new hub section : implement IDashboardModule (or derive from DashboardModule ) and add it to ModuleRegistry , or call ModuleRegistry.Register before the hub is shown. A section gives a view, a header, an order and a legend, and hands the D-pad's left and right edges to the hub with ForwardEdges . A new basic setting : add a BasicSetting to BasicSettings.All with Since one higher than the newest. Settings lists it, and the welcome screen opens once after the update that brings it, with it marked new. Telling more apps from games : add an ITitleClassifier to Library.Classifiers . Classifiers are asked in order and the first answer wins. Another content source : implement IContentSource , for example to list packages from a network share, and pass it to Library . A new view of titles : TileGrid takes any ITileTemplate . RowTemplate makes rows from a RowData description, and CoverTileTemplate makes covers.

docs.text: While the debug server is on (from the start in a Debug build; in a Release build once Settings > Debug server turns it on), it takes commands on TCP port 4601, one line each, and answers with a line of JSON: what the library holds, the console's functions called directly, memory, the log, what's on screen, button presses, frame rates and benchmarks of the dashboard's own work. Settings shows its address. The setting is kept, so a build deployed over one with it on starts with it on; it has no password, so anyone on the network can control the dashboard while it's on. python tests/run_tests.py 192.168.1.20 python tests/debugclient.py 192.168.1.20 The first runs the API, functional and performance tests against the console and can compare performance with an earlier run; the second is a shell for typing commands. See tests/README.md for the commands, the protocol and adding tests. To put a new build on the console and start it, over the dashboard's own FTP server and the debug server: python tools/deploy.py 192.168.1.20 -- --suite functional It finds where the dashboard runs from (else /Hdd1/Apps/Silverdash360 ), uploads only the files that changed, starts the new build through a staging folder so no running file is overwritten, checks it came up, and runs the tests given after -- . See Deploying a build .

docs.text: .\tools\Run.ps1 -Steps '16:shot' -Seconds 20 -ContentRoot gives xenia a content folder of its own, so the dashboard can be tried on a known set of packages without touching xenia's (see Testing in xenia ). The dashboard needs the XAM functions below, which xenia-edge doesn't have yet; they're on the pr-dashboard-content branch, to be proposed to xenia-edge. Function What the dashboard uses it for XamContentAggregateCreateEnumerator Every package of every title, as the console's dashboard lists them XamContentGetMetaDataInternal A package header's names, description and art XamContentLaunchImageInternalEx Starting a package xenia's hard drive has only its Content folder, so a build run from bin\Debug\xbox can't save its library, art or logs. To have it save them, install it under the content folder: -Install copies the build to <ContentRoot>\Silverdash360 and runs it from there, where the dashboard finds itself as /Hdd1/Content/Silverdash360 and keeps its data in Data beside it. -Fresh deletes that Data first, as a new install. .\tools\Run.ps1 -ContentRoot $env:TEMP\testcontent -Install -Fresh To sign a profile in at the start, pass --logged_profile_slot_0_xuid=<offline XUID> in -ExtraArgs ; xenia keeps the flags it's given in its config, so clear that line there to start with nobody signed in again. Signing in and out while the dashboard runs is xenia's Profile menu. The dashboard writes what it does to xenia's log as (DbgPrint) [Silverdash] ... . For the FTP server, run with --systemlink_transport=off (for example .\tools\Run.ps1 -ExtraArgs '--systemlink_transport=off' ): otherwise xenia's System Link emulation carries the dashboard's sockets and nothing listens on the PC. xenia moves port 21 to 10021, and the hard drive has only its Content folder there.

docs.text: Everything is C#. The console's own functions are called with DllImport by ordinal, with structures passed as pinned big-endian buffers. src/Silverdash360/ Native/ DllImports into xam.xex and xboxkrnl.exe, and NativeBuffer for structures Model/ ContentItem (one package), ContentMetadata (its header), TitleEntry, Gamer, ... Core/ Logging, background work, UiIdle (work that waits for the user), a JSON reader Services/ Library, LibraryCache, ProfileService, ImageService, ThemeService, UpdateService, ... Files/ XboxFileSystem: the drives as one tree of paths Ftp/ FtpServer, FtpSession and NativeSocket Media/ MediaService, the drive, DLNA and downloaded video sources, the local media server, an HTTP client Controls/ TileGrid (the virtualized grid), tile templates, OnScreenKeyboard, Theme Modules/ The hub's sections and the registry they're listed in Pages/ Hub, title details, search, storage, media, the player, pictures, files, themes, updates Debugging/ The debug server and its commands, on by default in Debug builds tests/ The tests that run over the debug server, and a client for it The library is read the way the console's dashboard reads it: Content : XamContentAggregateCreateEnumerator over every title, for common content and for the signed-in profile, returning 0x200-byte XCONTENT_DATA_INTERNAL records: of every type on a first start or a full refresh, otherwise of the types that start games and apps (see below). Metadata : XamContentGetMetaDataInternal per package, for names, description, publisher, version, size and thumbnails. Profile : XamUserGetSigninInfo , XamUserReadProfileSettings for the gamer card, XamUserCreateTitlesPlayedEnumerator and XamUserCreateAchievementEnumerator , and XamReadTile for game tiles and gamer pictures. Launching : XamContentLaunchImageInternalEx with the package's record, after checking it isn't partly downloaded or damaged. An executable from an Apps or Games folder starts with XamLoaderLaunchTitleEx and flags 0, with its folder as the D: drive. FTP : the console's Winsock ( NetDll_socket , bind , listen , accept , ...) on threads of its own, and the kernel's file calls on the drives' device paths. LibraryCache keeps the records and the header metadata in the Data folder of the folder the dashboard is installed in: the console's packages and the Apps and Games executables, the same whoever is signed in, in library.bin , and each profile's own packages (its saves and themes) in Profiles\<offline XUID>.bin . A package is the profile's when the profile's enumeration found it, whatever its record's XUID says. On a start the saved library is shown first, the console's packages with the signed-in profile's. Then only the types that start games and apps, with disc installs and themes, are listed again: on a console each type listed costs about 3 s however few packages it has, plus about 16 ms a package, and those are a few hundred of thousands. Add-ons, saves, avatar items, videos and the rest stay as saved; a title's page lists that title's packages again (an add-on holding an app, as Air Band is, keeps what was found in it), and Refresh library in settings lists everything. Only packages the files don't know have their headers read. With nobody signed in, only the console's are shown. A profile signing in or out from the Guide changes only the profile's part: the new profile's file and enumeration are read, the titles it and the old profile touch are built again (or copied, when only their played stats and saves change), and the console's packages stay as they are. A sign-in during a refresh pauses the refresh until the profile is shown. The debug server's library.profile times that step by step and checks it against a whole build. Reading the library, the art and the Marketplace pause while the user moves ( UiIdle ), and a save is written to a new file before the old one is replaced, so starting a game part way through doesn't lose it. Themes : the theme in use is kept per profile in Data\CurrentTheme\<offline XUID> : its wallpapers and the colours worked out from the first, with theme.txt naming the theme ( package:<title>/<file> or builtin:<n> ). A start reads only the profile's theme choice; when it names the kept theme, the wallpapers and colours come from there, without mounting the package or sampling a wallpaper again. Theme files don't change, so the name is all that's compared. The built-in themes' list is read from the DashPack ( \Device\Harddisk0\SystemExtPartition\Content\0000000000000000\FFFE07DF\00008000\FFFE07DF00000006 on a console) only when the theme picker wants it. A picture theme made in the Xbox Dashboard keeps its wallpaper as raw pixels rather than a JPEG: RGB , the width and height as big-endian words, then red, green and blue bytes a row at a time; WallpaperImage turns those into a WriteableBitmap 's pixels in the background. The theme picked is each profile's too, and nobody signed in's, in Data\ThemeChoice\<offline XUID or Nobody>.txt ; one with no pick follows the Xbox Dashboard's theme, which for nobody signed in is Silverdash's own look. Themes from the editor are kept per profile in Data\CustomTheme and, saved for everyone, in Data\SavedThemes . Media : the platform's player plays only from a URI, so the dashboard serves a file on a drive to it over HTTP on the console itself (port 4602, with a key made up at each start in every URL). A media server's files go through the same server, as the player won't play from another machine. Media servers are found with an SSDP search and browsed through their ContentDirectory; tests/dlna_server.py is a small one for trying it. Updates : the latest release comes from GitHub's API over HTTPS through the platform's HttpWebRequest ( github.com itself doesn't answer the console; api.github.com and its file storage do). The zip is checked against the release's size and SHA-256, its files written next to the dashboard's as .new , each running file renamed to .old (the system allows that for a file in use) and the new one put in its place; a failure puts the old ones back. A release's native image goes in only over the runtime its NativeImage.txt records; without it, the update renames an installed Silverdash360.ni.dll to .old as well, and the dashboard runs interpreted. The dashboard starts again, and the next start deletes the .old files. Debug builds don't look by themselves; the debug server's update.check , update.verify and update.install test it.

docs.text: A new hub section : implement IDashboardModule (or derive from DashboardModule ) and add it to ModuleRegistry , or call ModuleRegistry.Register before the hub is shown. A section gives a view, a header, an order and a legend, and hands the D-pad's left and right edges to the hub with ForwardEdges . A new basic setting : add a BasicSetting to BasicSettings.All with Since one higher than the newest. Settings lists it, and the welcome screen opens once after the update that brings it, with it marked new. Telling more apps from games : add an ITitleClassifier to Library.Classifiers . Classifiers are asked in order and the first answer wins. Another content source : implement IContentSource , for example to list packages from a network share, and pass it to Library . A new view of titles : TileGrid takes any ITileTemplate . RowTemplate makes rows from a RowData description, and CoverTileTemplate makes covers.

docs.text: Games and apps ¶ The games and apps sections are shelves of everything installed on the console's hard drive and USB drives. Each title has its box art from the Xbox Marketplace, where the console's own dashboard gets it, or the package's own picture. What's listed ¶ Xbox 360 games : installed discs, Games on Demand and Arcade, Indie and XNA games and demos. Original Xbox games , each one its own title. Apps , such as media apps, told apart from games by their title ID. Homebrew : a default.xex in each folder of a drive's Apps and Games folders ( Hdd1 , Usb0 to Usb2 ), and .xex files right in Apps . Each is named after its folder, unless a package or your profile names it. QuickBoot shortcuts show as the app or game they start; a shortcut and the folder it starts are listed once. Titles with nothing to start , such as a game with only saves or add-ons left, are hidden until you show them with the shelf's options. Silverdash360 keeps what it read, so it starts quickly. At a start it shows the library it saved and looks only for what starts games and apps, and for themes, as they come and go; a title's add-ons, updates and saves are listed again when you open its page. Refresh library in settings reads everything again. Box art and store details are downloaded in the background and kept in the Data\Art folder, so they're there without the internet afterwards. A title the Marketplace doesn't know gets a cover of its kind with its icon or its initials. Covers and lists ¶ Y switches a shelf between covers, two rows that scroll sideways, and a list with sizes and achievement progress. LT and RT move a screen at a time. A shelf sorted by name and long enough has a letter tile heading each letter's titles. A on a letter shows the letters alone, to jump through the shelf; A on a letter again shows everything, with that letter where it was. The shelf's options ¶ BACK on a shelf opens its options. A changes a setting, X steps it back, and B is done; the shelf follows at once and keeps them: Option Show Installed titles (the default), a kind (Xbox 360 games, Arcade, Indie and XNA, Demos, Original Xbox, Homebrew), the titles not installed, or everything Stored on A drive, or all of them Sort by Name, size or last played View Covers or a list A button Whether A plays a title or shows its details; START does the other A title's details ¶ A title's page has its backdrop, the store's description, developer, genre and release date, and two lists that LB and RB switch between: achievements , your progress in it, when you're signed in and have played it, and content , what's stored for it (the game, title updates, add-ons, saves) with sizes. Play starts it, with Play from disc when its disc is in the drive and a Play disc for each disc of a game with several; Achievements and Stored content go to the lists. Discs ¶ A disc in the drive comes first in jump back in, with a little disc on its cover. A game disc starts; a disc of files opens in media; a DVD movie, audio CD or original Xbox disc plays in the console's own player. For a game with several discs, its page has a Play disc for each. Y on home opens and closes the tray.

docs.text: Getting around ¶ Silverdash360 has six sections across the top: home , games , apps , media , me and settings . LB and RB go from one to the next at once, and round from settings to home. Moving past the left or right end of a section goes to the next one too, but only as a move of its own: holding the D-pad or the stick, or pressing it again and again to run through a shelf, stops at the shelf's end, and a press after a short pause goes on. The bar at the bottom says what the buttons do where you are. Controls ¶ Button D-pad, left stick Move A Play on home; open or select elsewhere. On the games and apps shelves, the shelf's options choose whether A plays or shows a title's details B Back START The other of A: a title's details on home; on the shelves, play or details, whichever A isn't X Search; your friends on me Y Open or close the disc tray on home; switch between covers and a list on the shelves; sign in on me BACK The shelf's options on the games and apps shelves LB, RB Switch sections, and lists and filters on other pages LT, RT A screen back or forward on the shelves Home ¶ Jump back in has the titles you played last, with the disc in the drive first. A starts a title, and START shows its details. Below it, apps has the apps installed. Y opens and closes the disc tray. Me ¶ Your gamertag, gamer picture, gamerscore, motto and zone, and the titles you've played with your progress in each. A shows a title's details, X your friends, and Y signs in, or signs in another profile. Silverdash360 works with nobody signed in: the games, apps and media are the console's. Signing in or out, here or from the Guide, shows that profile's saves, theme and played titles straight away, without reading the whole console again. Each profile keeps its own, and so does nobody signed in. Search ¶ X opens search from home and the shelves. Type with the on-screen keyboard (A types, X deletes, Y adds a space), and the results update as you type: titles by name, publisher or title ID. Move right to the results. When things are busy ¶ Silverdash360 puts what you do first: box art, wallpapers and reading the drives wait while you move, and catch up when you stop. A section you haven't opened yet is drawn once you stop on it.

docs.text: Installing ¶ Silverdash360 comes in two parts: a base package with everything it needs to run, from the Silverdash360 thread on Digiex , and the latest update's files from GitHub , which go over it. What you need ¶ An Xbox 360 that runs homebrew (RGH or JTAG). Silverdash360 isn't signed for a retail console, so it won't start on one. A way to copy files to the console , such as an FTP client or a USB drive. 1. Download the base package ¶ Download the base package, such as Silverdash360-0.1.2-console.zip , from the first post of the Silverdash360 thread on Digiex , and extract it. It has a Silverdash360 folder with everything Silverdash360 needs. 2. Add the latest update ¶ The base package isn't updated with every version, so add the newest one's files to it: Download the zip of the latest release on GitHub, such as Silverdash360-0.1.2.zip . Extract everything in it into the base package's Silverdash360 folder, replacing the files that are there. LICENSE.md , INSTALL.txt and NativeImage.txt can be left out. If the latest release has the same version as the base package, there's nothing to add. 3. Copy it to the console ¶ Copy the Silverdash360 folder to the console's hard drive, such as to Hdd1:\Apps\Silverdash360 , over FTP or from a USB drive. 4. Start it ¶ Start default.xex in that folder with your file manager or launcher. The first start welcomes you with a few basic settings, such as starting the FTP server with Silverdash360 (see Welcome screen ), and reads every package on the console, which takes a minute or two with a large collection; the games and apps fill in as it goes, and later starts are quick. Silverdash360 keeps its settings, the library it read and the box art it downloaded in a Data folder next to default.xex . Deleting Data starts it afresh. Next ¶ New versions install themselves when you say so: see Updating . To find your way around, see Getting around . To build Silverdash360 yourself, or make the base package from the app it runs on, see Development .

docs.text: Problems and ideas ¶ Problems and feature requests go to GitHub Issues , where they're kept track of until they're fixed or done. You need a GitHub account, which is free. For questions and talk about Silverdash360, there's the Silverdash360 thread on Digiex . Before you open one, look through the open issues in case it's there already. A 👍 on an issue says you'd like it too, and a comment can add what's different for you. Reporting a problem ¶ See Troubleshooting first. If it's not there, report the problem . The form asks for: What happened , and what you expected instead. How to make it happen : the section, page or title, and the buttons you pressed. The version : Version in settings, such as 0.1.2, build 77 (commit 3c4fe74) . Updating to the latest version first is worth it, in case it's fixed already. The console : System version in settings. The log , if you can: Data\Logs\silverdash.log.last in Silverdash360's folder, from the run that went wrong, or silverdash.log while it's still running. Copy it off with the FTP server and drag it into the form. It has your gamertag and the names of your games and apps in it. A screenshot or a photo of the screen helps too. Asking for a feature ¶ Request a feature : what you'd like Silverdash360 to do, and what it would help you with. How the Xbox Dashboard or another dashboard does it is useful to know. To fix or make it yourself, see Contributing : pull requests are welcome.

docs.text: Media ¶ The media section lists where your music, videos and pictures are: The drives : the hard drive, USB drives and a data disc. Media servers on your network that share over DLNA, such as Windows Media Player, Plex and Kodi. They're looked for when you stay on the media section. Downloaded videos : the movies, TV and trailers you downloaded from Xbox LIVE, with their pictures. A video downloaded since the last Refresh library in settings shows after the next one. Play disc , with a DVD movie or a game in the drive. A source opens as folders. LB and RB filter them: everything, music, videos or pictures. Playing ¶ A on a song or a video plays it, and then the rest of its kind in the folder, with the console's own transport bar; X and Y go to the previous and next. Pictures go left and right, and A starts a slideshow. Formats ¶ Silverdash360 plays what the console's player decodes: MP3, WMA and M4A (AAC) music, WMV, MP4, M4V and MOV (H.264) videos, and JPEG and PNG pictures. AAC and H.264 need the console's Optional Media Update, which the console installs the first time it's needed. Files in other formats, such as MKV and AVI, are listed dimmed with their format, and aren't played. The console's own dashboard plays AVI, MPEG-2 and audio CDs with players of its own, which apps can't use. Media servers ¶ A media server's files are played through Silverdash360, which fetches them for the console's player. If yours isn't listed: Check its DLNA sharing is on. In Plex it's Settings, DLNA, Enable the DLNA server . The console and the server need to be on the same network, and the network has to pass multicast, which some Wi-Fi setups block.

Themes ¶ The theme follows the console dashboard's own by default ( Same as the Xbox Dashboard ), so your wallpapers come with you. Theme lists the themes built into the console's dashboard and those installed on the console; A uses one. Each profile keeps the theme it picked, and so does nobody signed in: signing out shows the one picked with nobody signed in, or Silverdash360's own colours if none was. The built-in themes (Spectrum, Day and Night) are read from the console's own dashboard files, so they're the ones your dashboard version has; the dashboard's Xbox 360 theme isn't among those files, so Silverdash360 shows its own colours for it. A theme's four wallpapers go to the sections as they went to the first dashboard's blades: the first (Xbox Live's) to home, apps and me, the second to games, the third to media and the fourth (System's) to settings. Its colours go to Silverdash360's. Silverdash is Silverdash360's own colours and no wallpaper. Blades (Default) and Blades (Carbon) are colours after the two styles of the first Xbox 360 dashboard, with no wallpaper; as its blades did, each section has a colour of its own: me is Xbox Live's orange, games green, media blue, apps the Marketplace blade's and settings the System blade's. Picture themes made in the Xbox Dashboard from your own pictures work too. If the dashboard's theme for your profile is a theme package that's no longer installed, such as one from an older dashboard, Silverdash360 shows its own colours and settings names the missing theme. Theme editor ¶ Edit current theme , the first row of Theme , makes a theme of your own, starting from the one shown: Colours : the accent, secondary text, panels, the selected panel and the three colours of the background. A on one opens a grid of colours; the dashboard takes each on as you move, A keeps it and B puts the old one back. Wallpapers 1 to 4 : for home, apps and me, for games, for media, and for settings, as a theme's are. A wallpaper can be none, a JPEG or PNG picture on the console's drives (up to 4 MB), or any wallpaper of the built-in and installed themes, shown behind the list as you pick. Save makes it the custom theme of the profile signed in (or of nobody signed in, when nobody is) and uses it. Save for nobody signed in too also keeps it for when nobody is signed in. Save as... asks for a name and keeps it in Silverdash360 for everyone on the console; it's listed in Theme under that name. X on a saved theme there, twice, deletes it. B leaves without saving and puts the colours back. Once saved, Custom theme in the theme list picks it again; it's listed for a profile that has one, or for nobody signed in when there's one for nobody. Storage ¶ Everything stored on the console, largest first, by kind: games, apps, add-ons, title updates, saves and media. LB and RB filter it. A opens the title a package belongs to. Add-ons and saves are as Silverdash360 last read them: when you opened their title's page, or at the last Refresh library . File browser ¶ Every folder and file on the console's drives. A opens a folder, plays a song, video or picture, or starts a .xex . A content package shows its name and picture. FTP server ¶ The FTP server shares the console's drives while Silverdash360 runs. FTP server turns it on and off with A, and shows the address, user name and password while it's on. With Start the FTP server with Silverdash on, it starts by itself each time. The user name is xbox and the password six digits made up at the first start; both stay the same until you change them. A on FTP user name or FTP password opens the console's keyboard to change it. Connect with plain FTP, such as FileZilla with Only use plain FTP ; there's no TLS. Each drive is a folder: Hdd1 , Usb0 to Usb2 , Mu0 , Mu1 and Dvd (read only). You can download, upload, rename and delete, and make and remove folders. FTP sends the password unencrypted, so use it on a network you trust. Debug server ¶ Debug server , the last setting, turns on a TCP port (4601) that takes commands from a PC: what tests, tools\deploy.py and the other tools in the repository use (see Debug server and tests ). A turns it on and off at once, and it stays as you left it the next time Silverdash360 starts. It's off unless you turn it on; builds made for testing have it on. It has no password. While it's on, anyone on your network can control Silverdash360, read the files on the console's drives and start programs. Leave it off unless you're testing or developing, and then use it on a network you trust.

See Installing . A runtime you made yourself has to come from Plex v0.0.0.7: see The runtime . The console has to run homebrew. A game or app is missing ¶ The shelves show installed titles only. BACK on the shelf, Show , Everything shows the rest too. Refresh library in settings reads every package again. Homebrew is looked for in the Apps and Games folders of Hdd1 and Usb0 to Usb2 , a folder each with a default.xex in it. An add-on, save or downloaded video is missing ¶ A start looks only for new games, apps and themes. A title's add-ons, updates and saves are read again when you open its page; Refresh library in settings reads everything, downloaded videos too. The box art or the theme is missing ¶ Box art comes from the Xbox Marketplace the first time a title is shown, so the console needs the internet once. The first time, or after picking another, it shows once its package has been found. Each profile has its own theme, and so has nobody signed in: see Themes . docs.text: Updating ¶ Silverdash360 looks for a new version on GitHub a few seconds after it starts, once you've left the controller alone for a moment. It needs the console to be on the internet; it doesn't need Xbox LIVE. When there's a new version, it shows what's new in it and asks: Choice Update now Downloads the new version, installs it and starts it. It takes a few seconds. Later (or B) Asks again the next time Silverdash360 starts. Skip this version Doesn't ask about this version again. A newer one is offered as usual. Check for updates in settings looks any time, and offers a version you skipped too. How an update installs ¶ The update is checked against the release on GitHub before anything is changed: its size and its SHA-256 must match. Silverdash360 then puts each new file next to the one it replaces, swaps them, and starts again. The release's native image, Silverdash360.ni.dll (Silverdash360's code compiled with XboxNGen , which runs much faster), goes in only when the console has the runtime it was compiled for, the base package's; otherwise Silverdash360 leaves it out and runs without it, slower. If a step fails, the old files are put back and it carries on as it was. Your settings and library in the Data folder stay as they are. Updating by hand ¶ Download the zip of the latest release and copy what's in it over the files in Silverdash360's folder on the console, replacing them. The runtime files stay as they are. If you installed Silverdash360 over a runtime you made yourself rather than the base package, and it isn't the same as the one NativeImage.txt lists, leave Silverdash360.ni.dll out: Silverdash360 doesn't start with it over another runtime. Version 0.1.0 doesn't look for updates, so updating from it to 0.1.1 or later is done by hand once. Which version you have ¶ Version in settings shows it, such as 0.1.1, build 50 (commit 80c3ccc) .
